title: Shared jeep or reserved car: when each makes sense
meta_description: Shared jeep or reserved car in Darjeeling and Sikkim? Fares, comfort, timing and safety compared, with the legs where each one wins. Indicative 2026 prices.
summary: Take a shared jeep for point-to-point transfers between towns when you travel light and in a group of one to three. Take a reserved car for sunrise trips, permit areas, families with children or seniors, and any day with several stops. Most good budget trips use both.
key_takeaways: Shared jeeps cost ₹250–600 a seat on the main routes from Siliguri, against ₹3,500–6,500 for a whole reserved car, indicative 2026.
For one to three people, shared jeeps save a lot; at four or more, a reserved car is close in cost per head.
Sightseeing days, Tiger Hill at dawn, Tsomgo and North Sikkim need a reserved or package vehicle anyway.
Shared jeeps leave when full, carry 10 or more people and have little room for big bags, so pack light.

sections.heading: How the shared jeep system works
paras: Ask anyone who grew up in Darjeeling or Gangtok how they got to Siliguri as a child, and the answer will be a shared jeep. These are Mahindra Boleros, Tata Sumos and similar vehicles that run fixed routes between towns, leaving from a stand when every seat is sold. A full vehicle usually carries 10 passengers: two beside the driver, four in the middle and four on the back benches, and bags go on the roof under a tarpaulin.

Fares are set by the local syndicates and are posted at most stands. You buy a ticket at the counter, often with your name written on a list, and wait. On busy routes such as Siliguri to Darjeeling or Siliguri to Gangtok, jeeps leave every 15–30 minutes from early morning until early afternoon. On quieter routes, such as Darjeeling to Pelling, there may be only one or two a day, so it pays to ask at the stand the evening before.

You can also buy more than one seat. Many couples buy the full front bench, two seats beside the driver, for more room and the best view. Some groups buy all ten seats, which is called reserving the jeep and costs close to a reserved car.

sections.heading: Prices on the main routes
paras: These are the fares we see most often in 2026. Shared fares are per seat; reserved fares are for the whole vehicle, usually a small car or a Bolero, with an Innova costing more. All are indicative, rise in peak weeks, and change with fuel prices, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: When the shared jeep wins
paras: The shared jeep is the right choice on a straight transfer from one town to the next, when you have no stops to make and you are travelling light. For a solo traveller or a couple, the saving is large. Two people going from NJP to Gangtok pay ₹800–1,200 in a shared jeep against ₹4,000–6,000 for a car. Over a 6-night trip with three transfer days, that can be ₹8,000–12,000 saved for a couple.

It is also often faster than you expect. Shared drivers know the road, do not stop for photos, and many of them have driven the same route daily for years. And it is a good way to meet people: students going home, tea garden staff, monks, nurses, shopkeepers with boxes of vegetables. We have learned more about road conditions from the front bench than from any website.
list: Solo travellers, couples and groups of three
Transfer days with no sightseeing on the way
Travellers with one backpack or small suitcase each
Routes with frequent departures: Siliguri to Darjeeling, Gangtok, Kalimpong

sections.heading: When a reserved car is worth it
paras: Some days need your own vehicle. Tiger Hill at 4 am has no shared service worth the name. Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La from Gangtok are permit areas where tourists go by reserved car or by shared seat in a tour vehicle arranged by an agent, not by public jeep. North Sikkim trips to Lachung and Lachen run as packages with a vehicle, driver and permit together. Check current status before you travel.

A reserved car also makes sense for families. Small children, seniors and anyone prone to motion sickness do much better when they can stop, sit in front and leave when they are ready. Large suitcases, a pram or a wheelchair will not fit on a shared jeep roof safely.

Finally, look at the maths for groups of four or more. Four people on a shared jeep to Darjeeling pay ₹1,000–1,600 between them; a reserved car is ₹3,500–4,500. The gap shrinks to a few hundred rupees per person, and you get door-to-door pick-up and the freedom to stop at Kurseong or a tea garden on the way.

sections.heading: Comfort, timing and safety
paras: Comfort is the main trade-off. The back benches of a shared jeep face sideways, have little legroom and feel every bend. If you are sensitive to motion, ask for a front seat when you buy your ticket, and pay for two if you need the room. Middle-row window seats are the next best.

Timing matters too. Shared jeeps run mainly in the morning and early afternoon. The last jeeps up the hill from Siliguri usually leave by 3–4 pm, and fewer run on the day of a local strike or holiday. If your train reaches NJP late, plan for a reserved car or a night in Siliguri.

On safety, the main shared routes are driven by experienced local drivers, and the jeeps run as registered commercial vehicles under the transport rules of West Bengal and Sikkim. Use the official stands and counters, not a driver who approaches you on the platform. Keep valuables on your lap, not in a roof bag. In monsoon, ask at the counter whether the road is open before you buy a ticket.

sections.heading: A few words of shared-jeep etiquette
paras: Shared jeeps run on habits that locals know and visitors learn quickly. Be at the stand 15 minutes before you want to leave, and keep your ticket handy, because the driver or a stand clerk will call names from a list. If you buy the front seats, say so at the counter; they cannot be claimed by sitting in them first.

Drivers stop once or twice on long routes, usually at a roadside tea stall where ₹20–40 buys tea and a snack. Use these stops, because there may not be another for two hours. Ask before you open a window wide in winter, and keep your music on headphones. If you feel unwell on the bends, tell the driver early; most will pull over for a minute without fuss.
Finally, carry small notes. Counters and drivers often have little change, especially early in the morning, and a ₹2,000 note for a ₹300 seat will not make you friends.

sections.heading: Our rule of thumb
paras: On most budget trips we plan, the pattern is simple. Shared jeeps for the long transfer days between Siliguri and the hills and between towns. A reserved car for the one or two days that need it: Tiger Hill and local sightseeing in Darjeeling, Tsomgo from Gangtok. Local shared taxis, at ₹20–60 a seat, for short hops within Gangtok or between Darjeeling and Ghum.

That mix gives you most of the savings of travelling like a local, with none of the stress of trying to reach a sunrise viewpoint by public transport. For a couple on a 5-night Darjeeling and Gangtok trip, it usually saves ₹6,000–9,000 compared with a reserved car on every leg.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from NJP to Darjeeling
faqs.a: A shared jeep seat from NJP or Siliguri to Darjeeling costs about ₹250–400, indicative 2026, and the trip takes 3–3.5 hours. Jeeps leave when full from stands near NJP station and on Hill Cart Road in Siliguri, mostly between early morning and mid-afternoon. A whole reserved car costs about ₹3,500–4,500.

faqs.q: Is a shared jeep safe for women travelling alone
faqs.a: Yes, on the main routes it is widely used by local women, students and families every day. Buy your ticket at the official counter, ask for a front or window seat, and keep valuables on your lap. Avoid the last jeep of the day if it would bring you in after dark, and tell your hotel your expected arrival time.

faqs.q: Can I take big suitcases on a shared jeep
faqs.a: Usually one medium suitcase per person goes on the roof under a tarpaulin, sometimes with a small luggage charge. Very large suitcases, several bags each or fragile items are a problem, and there is no room inside. Families with heavy luggage are better off in a reserved car, which takes bags in the boot or on the roof.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to reserve a car for four people
faqs.a: It is close. Four shared seats from Siliguri to Darjeeling cost ₹1,000–1,600 in total against ₹3,500–4,500 for a reserved car, indicative 2026. The difference is about ₹500–750 per person, and the car gives you door-to-door pick-up, stops on the way and room for bags. For five or more, the car is usually the better deal.

faqs.q: Can I go to Tsomgo Lake by shared jeep
faqs.a: Not by public shared jeep. Tsomgo is in a protected area that needs a permit arranged by a registered Gangtok travel agent, and you go either in a reserved car or in a shared seat in an agent's tour vehicle, about ₹800–1,300 a seat, indicative 2026. Check current status before you travel.
